content.content:
## The Multilingual World

Here is a fact that surprises many people in monolingual societies: speaking just one language is the exception, not the rule. More than half of the world's population uses two or more languages in daily life. In many parts of Africa, South Asia, and Southeast Asia, it is entirely normal to speak three, four, or even five languages. Even in Europe, where monolingualism has been more common, multilingualism is growing fast thanks to migration, globalisation, and education.

It helps to distinguish two kinds. **Individual multilingualism** is a person's ability to use two or more languages -- ranging from near-native fluency in all to strong ability in one and limited skills in others. **Societal multilingualism** is the presence of multiple languages within a country or community, and a society can be multilingual even if most individuals are monolingual, as in Belgium, where different regions speak different languages. Examples abound: India has 22 officially recognised languages; Singapore has four official languages; Luxembourg has three plus widespread English; South Africa has 11; and even Norway has two written standards (Bokmål and Nynorsk), Sami languages, and increasingly English as a de facto second language.

## The Many Faces of Bilingualism

Bilingualism is not one thing -- it comes in many forms, and the distinctions matter. **Additive bilingualism** means learning a second language while maintaining and developing the first; it is associated with cognitive benefits and positive outcomes, like a Norwegian child learning English at school while continuing to develop Norwegian at home. **Subtractive bilingualism** means learning a second language at the expense of the first, which gradually weakens -- associated with negative outcomes, as when an immigrant child's first language is not supported at school. **Simultaneous bilingualism** means acquiring two languages from birth, while **sequential bilingualism** means adding a second language after the first is established. **Receptive bilingualism** means understanding a language without speaking it fluently -- common in Scandinavia, where many Norwegians understand Swedish and Danish without speaking them. And there is a social dimension too: **elite bilingualism** (by choice, often through education and travel) contrasts with **folk bilingualism** (arising from necessity, such as immigration or minority status).

Why does any of this matter? Because research suggests real cognitive advantages to being bilingual. Bilinguals often outperform monolinguals on tasks requiring **executive function** -- attention control, cognitive flexibility, and working memory -- because constantly managing two languages strengthens the brain's control system. Several large studies have found that bilingual individuals develop symptoms of dementia and Alzheimer's around 4-5 years later than monolinguals, suggesting a "cognitive reserve" built through lifelong bilingualism. Bilinguals also tend to have better **metalinguistic awareness** -- a sharper understanding of how language works. Important caveats apply: the "bilingual advantage" has been debated, some studies fail to replicate it, and socioeconomic factors can confound results. But the broad picture is that multilingualism is cognitively healthy.

## Language Policy: Who Decides Which Languages Thrive

Every country has **language policies** -- explicit or implicit rules about which languages are used in government, education, media, and public life. These policies profoundly shape which languages flourish and which decline.

There are several types. **Official monolingualism** designates one language as the sole official one, as in France, where French is the only official language and regional languages like Breton and Occitan have been marginalised. **Official multilingualism** recognises several, as in Switzerland (German, French, Italian, Romansh), Canada (English, French), and India. **Language-in-education policy** determines which languages are used to teach and which are taught as subjects -- Norway, for instance, requires all students to learn both Bokmål and Nynorsk plus English. **Assimilation policies** have historically pressured minority groups to abandon their languages, as with the forced assimilation of the Sami in Norway and indigenous peoples in Australia and the Americas. And increasingly, **language rights** are recognised as human rights, including the right to education in one's mother tongue.

A few precise terms help here. An **official language** has legal status for public administration. The **medium of instruction (MOI)** is the language used to teach subjects -- a critical factor for multilingual students. **Mother-tongue education** teaches children in their first language, at least in the early years, and research consistently shows it produces better outcomes. **Language planning** is deliberate effort to influence a language's structure, function, or acquisition; it splits into **corpus planning** (developing the language itself -- new vocabulary, dictionaries, standardised grammar) and **status planning** (changing a language's social role, such as making it official). The thread running through all of this is that **linguistic human rights** -- the right to use, maintain, and develop one's language without discrimination -- are increasingly recognised internationally.

## Summary

Multilingualism is the global norm -- more than half the world's population speaks multiple languages. **Individual multilingualism** ranges from balanced bilingualism to receptive knowledge, and includes distinctions like **additive** versus **subtractive** and **simultaneous** versus **sequential** bilingualism. **Additive bilingualism** is linked to cognitive benefits such as stronger executive function, possibly delayed dementia, and enhanced **metalinguistic awareness**, though some findings are debated. **Language policy** -- whether official monolingualism, official multilingualism, or assimilation -- profoundly shapes which languages thrive, and **mother-tongue education** is consistently supported by research. Through **language planning** (both **corpus** and **status** planning) and the growing recognition of **linguistic human rights**, societies decide the fate of their languages -- a decision with deep consequences for individuals and communities alike.
